lessons.title: Mounting Front Brake Caliper and Rotor
lessons.body:
Start by gathering your tools: 5mm and 6mm Allen keys, 10mm and 12mm spanners, a torque wrench, threadlocker (blue), and a clean rag. Put the motorbike on a stable stand so the front wheel is off the ground. Remove the wheel if your model requires it; otherwise, work with it in place. First, clean the rotor with brake cleaner and a lint-free cloth to remove any oil. Slide the rotor onto the hub, aligning the bolt holes. Apply a drop of threadlocker to each rotor bolt, then tighten them in a star pattern to 12â15 Nm. Don't overtightenâyou can warp the rotor.

Next, mount the caliper. If the caliper bracket is separate, bolt it to the fork leg first, using the original bolts and threadlocker. Tighten to 20â25 Nm. Then slide the caliper over the rotor, making sure the brake pads are seated correctly and the rotor sits centered between them. If the pads are new, you may need to push the pistons back gently with a flat screwdriver before fitting. Bolt the caliper to the bracket or fork, and tighten to 25â30 Nm. Spin the wheelâit should turn freely with a slight drag from the pads. If it locks or rubs hard, the caliper may not be centered; loosen the mounting bolts, wiggle the caliper, and retighten.

In many African workshops, you'll work with basic hand tools, so always use the correct size to avoid stripping bolts. If you don't have a torque wrench, tighten firmly but not with extreme forceâstripped threads are a common problem. After mounting, pump the brake lever a few times to seat the pads. Check for leaks at the caliper banjo bolt. A properly mounted front brake is critical for safety, especially on rough roads. Test by spinning the wheel and applying the brake; it should stop the wheel smoothly. If you hear grinding, check pad alignment. Finally, recheck all bolts after the first ride.

lessons.title: Installing Rear Brake Caliper and Rotor
lessons.body:
The rear brake setup is similar to the front but often has less space and may include a mechanical parking brake on some EV models. You'll need the same tools: Allen keys, spanners, torque wrench, threadlocker, and brake cleaner. Start by supporting the rear wheel off the ground. Remove the rear wheel if necessaryâon many electric motorbikes, you must disconnect the motor cable first. Clean the rear rotor and hub. Mount the rotor onto the hub, applying threadlocker to the bolts. Tighten in a star pattern to 12â15 Nm. If the rotor is warped, replace it; a warped rotor causes pulsating brakes.

Now, attach the caliper bracket to the swingarm or axle mount. Use new bolts if the old ones are corroded. Apply threadlocker and tighten to 20â25 Nm. Slide the caliper over the rotor, ensuring the pads are correctly positioned. On some models, you need to remove the pads to fit the caliper, then reinsert them. Push the pistons back if they are extended. Bolt the caliper to the bracket and tighten to 25â30 Nm. Spin the wheel; it should rotate with a slight drag. If the wheel is hard to turn, the caliper may be misaligned. Loosen the mounting bolts, center the caliper by eye, and retighten.

For EVs with regenerative braking, the rear brake may be used less, but it must still work perfectly as a backup. After installation, pump the brake pedal or lever to build pressure. Check for fluid leaks at the caliper and banjo bolt. If the brake feels spongy, you'll need to bleed the system (covered in a later lesson). In rural areas, dust and mud can quickly contaminate brake pads, so ensure the caliper is not rubbing. Test the brake by riding slowly and applying it; the bike should stop smoothly without pulling to one side. Recheck bolt tightness after your first ride, as vibration can loosen them.

lessons.title: Connecting Brake Lines and Bleeding
lessons.body:
Brake lines carry hydraulic fluid from the master cylinder to the caliper. If you're installing new lines, use copper washers on both sides of the banjo bolt. Start by connecting the line to the master cylinder first, then to the caliper. Tighten the banjo bolts to 20â25 Nmâtoo loose and it leaks, too tight and you crush the washer. Use a clean syringe or a small funnel to fill the master cylinder reservoir with DOT 3 or DOT 4 brake fluid. Never mix different types. Keep the reservoir topped up during bleeding to avoid air entering.

Bleeding removes air from the system. You'll need an 8mm spanner, a clear plastic tube, and a container for old fluid. Place the tube over the bleeder nipple on the caliper and submerge the other end in a little brake fluid. Pump the brake lever several times and hold it. Open the bleeder nipple a quarter turnâfluid and air bubbles will flow out. Close the nipple before releasing the lever. Repeat until no bubbles appear and the lever feels firm. Check the fluid level in the reservoir often; if it runs dry, you'll have to start over. In hot African climates, brake fluid absorbs moisture quickly, so use fresh fluid from a sealed container.

If you don't have a bleeding kit, you can use a clean bottle and tube. Work in a well-ventilated area; brake fluid damages paint and is toxic. After bleeding, top up the reservoir to the MAX line and replace the diaphragm and cap. Test the brake leverâit should feel solid, not spongy. If it's still spongy, there may be air trapped; try tapping the caliper and lines to dislodge bubbles and bleed again. Check all connections for leaks. A proper bleed is essential for safe braking, especially on steep hills. Always dispose of old brake fluid responsiblyânever pour it on the ground.

lessons.title: Adjusting Brake Lever Free Play
lessons.body:
Brake lever free play is the small amount of movement before the brake starts to engage. Too much free play and the brake feels vague; too little and the brake may drag, overheating the pads. For most motorbikes, the recommended free play at the lever end is 10â20mm. Check by pulling the lever lightly until you feel resistance; measure the gap between the lever and the handlebar grip. On cable-operated brakes, adjust using the knurled nut at the lever or the adjuster near the caliper. Loosen the lock nut, turn the adjuster out to reduce free play or in to increase it. Tighten the lock nut and recheck.

For hydraulic brakes, free play is not adjustable at the lever; it's set by the master cylinder. If there's excessive play, it may indicate air in the system or a worn master cylinder. Bleed the brakes first. If the lever still has too much play, the master cylinder may need rebuilding. On some EVs, the brake lever also activates a switch for the brake light or regenerative braking. Ensure the switch clicks just as the brake engages. Adjust the switch position if needed.

In African workshops, riders often prefer a slightly firmer lever for better control on rough roads. However, never set free play to zero; the brake will drag and overheat. After adjustment, spin the wheel and apply the brakeâit should stop the wheel without rubbing when released. Test ride at low speed to ensure the brake engages smoothly. If the lever feels spongy, bleed again. Regularly check free play as part of your maintenance routine. A well-adjusted brake lever improves safety and reduces fatigue on long rides.

lessons.title: Testing Brake Function and Safety
lessons.body:
After installing and adjusting your brakes, you must test them thoroughly before riding on public roads. Start with a static test: with the bike on a stand, spin each wheel and apply the brake. The wheel should stop immediately and not rub when released. Check the brake lever and pedal for firmnessâif they feel spongy, bleed the system. Inspect all connections for leaks; a drop of fluid under the caliper or master cylinder means a loose banjo bolt or a damaged seal. Tighten or replace as needed.

Next, do a low-speed test in a safe area, like an empty yard or quiet street. Ride at walking pace and apply the front brake gently, then the rear. The bike should slow smoothly without pulling to one side. If it pulls, one caliper may be sticking or the rotor may be warped. Increase speed to about 20 km/h and brake harder. You should feel a progressive bite. If the brake grabs or locks suddenly, the pads may be contaminated with oil or the rotor may be glazed. Clean or replace as necessary. Test the brakes on different surfacesâtarmac, dirt, gravelâto simulate African road conditions.

Check the brake light: it should come on when you apply the brake. For EVs, ensure the regenerative braking engages without interfering with hydraulic braking. After testing, let the brakes cool and recheck bolt tightnessâvibration can loosen caliper bolts. Look for signs of overheating, like blueing on the rotor or a burning smell. If you find any issue, fix it before riding further. Remember, brakes are your most important safety system. Never compromise. Carry out these tests after any brake work, and repeat them periodically. A well-tested brake system gives you confidence on any road.

lessons.title: Parking Brake Integration (if applicable)
lessons.body:
Some electric motorbikes, especially cargo models, come with a mechanical parking brake that locks the rear wheel when parked. This is often a lever or pedal that engages a separate caliper or a locking pin in the rear brake. If your bike has one, you'll need to integrate it with the hydraulic brake system. Start by identifying the parking brake mechanismâit could be a cable-operated caliper or a mechanical lock on the main caliper. Install the parking brake caliper or bracket according to the manufacturer's instructions, using threadlocker on all bolts and tightening to specified torque, usually 20â25 Nm.

If the parking brake uses a cable, route it along the frame, avoiding sharp bends and hot parts. Adjust the cable so that when engaged, the rear wheel cannot turn. There should be a small amount of free play in the lever when disengaged. Test by engaging the parking brake, then trying to push the bikeâit should not move. Disengage and ensure the wheel spins freely. If the parking brake is integrated into the main caliper, it may use a mechanical screw that pushes the pads. Follow the service manual for adjustment. In many African settings, parking brakes are essential on hills; a failed parking brake can cause the bike to roll away.

After installation, test the parking brake on a slope. Engage it, put the bike in gear (if applicable), and try to roll it. It should hold firmly. Check that the brake disengages fully when released; otherwise, the pads will drag and overheat. Lubricate the cable or mechanism with a little grease. Regularly inspect the parking brake for wear. If it's not applicable to your model, skip this lesson, but always use the main brake when parking. For EVs without a parking brake, you can leave the bike in gear (if it has a transmission) or use a strap. Never rely solely on the motor's resistance to hold the bike.

quiz.q: What is the recommended torque for front brake rotor bolts?
quiz.explanation: Rotor bolts typically require 12-15 Nm to avoid warping the rotor.

quiz.q: Which tool is essential for tightening brake caliper bolts to the correct specification?
quiz.explanation: A torque wrench ensures bolts are tightened to the manufacturer's specified torque.

quiz.q: What should you apply to rotor bolts before installation?
quiz.explanation: Threadlocker prevents bolts from loosening due to vibration.

quiz.q: When mounting the front caliper, what should you check after tightening the bolts?
options: A) Wheel spins freely with slight drag
quiz.explanation: A slight drag indicates the pads are contacting the rotor but not binding.

quiz.q: What is a common problem if you overtighten caliper bolts?
quiz.explanation: Overtightening can strip threads, warp the rotor, or cause leaks.

quiz.q: Before installing the rear brake caliper, what should you do if the pistons are extended?
quiz.explanation: Pushing the pistons back allows the caliper to fit over the rotor.

quiz.q: What is the recommended torque for rear caliper mounting bolts?
quiz.explanation: Caliper mounting bolts typically require 20-25 Nm.

quiz.q: Why should you clean the rotor before installation?
options: A) To remove oil and dirt
quiz.explanation: Oil or dirt on the rotor reduces braking performance.

quiz.q: What should you do if the rear wheel is hard to turn after installing the caliper?
options: A) Loosen the caliper bolts and center it
quiz.explanation: Misalignment causes drag; centering the caliper fixes it.

quiz.q: What type of brake fluid is commonly used in motorbike hydraulic brakes?
quiz.explanation: DOT 3 or DOT 4 brake fluid is standard for hydraulic systems.

quiz.q: When bleeding brakes, why must you keep the reservoir topped up?
quiz.explanation: If the reservoir runs dry, air enters the system and bleeding must be restarted.

quiz.q: What is the correct order for bleeding a brake system?
options: A) Pump lever, hold, open bleeder, close bleeder, release lever
B) Open bleeder, pump lever, close bleeder
C) Pump lever, open bleeder, release lever
D) Open bleeder, release lever, pump lever
quiz.explanation: This sequence forces fluid and air out without reintroducing air.

quiz.q: How can you tell if there is still air in the brake system after bleeding?
quiz.explanation: Air in the system makes the lever feel spongy.

quiz.q: What should you do with old brake fluid?
quiz.explanation: Brake fluid is toxic and must be disposed of properly.

quiz.q: What is the recommended free play at the brake lever for most motorbikes?
quiz.explanation: 10-20mm free play ensures the brake engages properly without dragging.

quiz.q: How do you adjust free play on a cable-operated brake?
quiz.explanation: The knurled adjuster changes cable tension, altering free play.

quiz.q: What can cause excessive free play in a hydraulic brake lever?
quiz.explanation: Air in the system or worn pads can increase lever travel.

quiz.q: Why should you never set brake lever free play to zero?
options: A) Brake will drag and overheat
quiz.explanation: Zero free play causes the brake to drag, leading to overheating.

quiz.q: What should you check after adjusting the brake lever?
options: A) Wheel spins freely when brake released
quiz.explanation: Both free wheel rotation and brake light function are important.

quiz.q: What is a sign of a properly bled brake system?
quiz.explanation: A firm lever indicates no air in the system.

quiz.q: During a static brake test, what should happen when you apply the brake?
quiz.explanation: The brake should stop the wheel without rubbing when released.

quiz.q: If the bike pulls to one side when braking, what is a likely cause?
quiz.explanation: A sticking caliper or warped rotor can cause uneven braking.

quiz.q: What should you do if brake pads are contaminated with oil?
quiz.explanation: Contaminated pads cannot be reliably cleaned and should be replaced.

quiz.q: Why should you recheck brake bolts after a test ride?
quiz.explanation: Vibration from riding can cause bolts to loosen.

quiz.q: What is a common sign of overheated brakes?
quiz.explanation: Overheating causes blueing and a burning smell.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a parking brake on an electric motorbike?
options: A) To hold the bike when parked
quiz.explanation: A parking brake locks the wheel to prevent rolling when parked.

quiz.q: How should a parking brake cable be routed?
options: A) Avoiding sharp bends and hot parts
quiz.explanation: Proper routing prevents binding and heat damage.

quiz.q: When the parking brake is engaged, what should happen?
quiz.explanation: The parking brake should lock the rear wheel to hold the bike.

quiz.q: What should you do if the parking brake does not disengage fully?
quiz.explanation: Adjustment ensures the brake releases completely to prevent drag.

quiz.q: Why is it important to test the parking brake on a slope?
options: A) To ensure it holds the bike
quiz.explanation: Testing on a slope verifies the parking brake can prevent rolling.
